title: Arguments from consciousness and reason
note: These arguments claim that minds fit poorly into a purely physical world. The argument from consciousness says subjective experience is more to be expected if God exists. The argument from reason (Lewis) and Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism say that if naturalism were true, we would lack good reason to trust the very reasoning that leads to naturalism.

read.title: Can naturalism trust itself?
text: Alvin Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism (EAAN) does not attack evolution. It argues that naturalism (N) combined with evolution (E) undermines itself. Let R be the claim that our cognitive faculties are reliable, mostly producing true beliefs.

(1) The probability of R, given N and E, is low or inscrutable. (2) Anyone who accepts N and E, and sees that (1) is true, has a defeater for R. (3) A defeater for R is a defeater for every belief one's faculties produce, including N and E. (4) So accepting N and E is self-defeating, and cannot rationally be held.

Premise (1) rests on this thought: natural selection rewards adaptive behavior, not true belief. If, on naturalism, a belief causes behavior by its brain chemistry rather than by its content, selection would not care whether that content is true. Darwin himself, in an 1881 letter, voiced a 'horrid doubt' about trusting a mind descended from lower animals.

The main objection, from William Ramsey and Jerry Fodor among others, is that true beliefs generally help us survive. An animal that believes 'a tiger is near' when a tiger is near will tend to live longer.

Plantinga replies that this assumes what is in question: that content, not mere neurophysiology, causes behavior. On materialism, he argues, that is exactly what is hard to secure; theism, by contrast, gives a reason to expect minds made to know truth.

Why does premise (3) extend the defeater to N and E?
o: N and E are themselves products of our faculties
